newsitem.title: CHILE: FOCUS - Codelco, Merrill end copper futures dispute.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Codelco, Merrill end copper futures dispute.

text.p: Merrill Lynch and Co Inc agreed Tuesday to pay Chilean state copper giant Codelco $25 million to settle a dispute resulting from a copper futures trading scandal which shook world metals markets in 1994.

Codelco's former top futures trader Juan Pablo Davila was fired after the corporation lost some $170 million in trades gone sour that he carried out with European and U.S. copper brokers, including Merrill Lynch.

"Although Merrill Lynch denies having done anything incorrect, it will pay Codelco $25 million to put an end to this dispute and avoid the costs that are involved in continuing," said Codelco president Marcos Lima, who read a joint statement from both companies.
Merrill's payment will include $22 million to cover Codelco's losses and $3 million towards its legal costs.
The settlement is the first Codelco has made in its three-year probe into Davila's deals, which stained its name and forced the resignation in disgrace of its then-president.
Codelco, the world's largest copper producer, has court cases pending in London against Belgian and German brokers, accusing them of allegedly paying secret commissions to Davila.

"The agreement is important for Codelco as it shows that they are still pursuing this," said one copper trader at a foreign trading firm in Santiago. "They've come under criticism for not nailing anyone."
One aim of the deal is to restore normal trading relations between Codelco and Merrill Lynch, Codelco's primary broker before the scandal broke in early 1994.

"Merrill has been very keen to rebuild the relationship with Codelco. They want to repair bridges," said the trader. The statement said Codelco's probe had failed to find evidence of illicit payments by Merrill Lynch to the once high-flying trader, who was fired as soon as the losses were discovered.
The two companies entered into talks to reach a settlement in December 1995 after Codelco told Merrill that it planned to start legal action against the brokerage.
The claim was based on charges that "ex-employees of Merrill Lynch by action or ommission facilitated Juan Pablo Davila's unauthorized speculative operations," said the statement.
"We believed we had a very strong claim against Merrill Lynch and we communicated that to Merrill Lynch very firmly," Codelco's U.S. lawyer Philip Forlenza told the news conference.
"We explained that if this matter was not settled, we would file the claim."
Under the terms of the deal, Merrill gave Codelco access to tape recordings, documents and personnel to check the broker's assertion that it had not made any payments to Davila.
Codelco has issued writs in London against Belgian traders Sogemin and Germany's Metallgesellschaft and its former copper trader Wolfgang Becker. Both companies and Becker have denied any wrongdoing.
Becker worked for Metallgesellschaft while Davila was trading with the firm and later moved to run Merrill Lynch's Hamburg office. He resigned from Merrill Lynch in 1995.
Davila, who was fired when the losses were uncovered in 1994, has been charged with fraud and carrying out business "incompatible" with his position in Codelco.
He was recently released from preventive detention in a Santiago jail to undergo cancer treatment.
